options: Deleting old logs to save storage space
Pulling logs from many different sources -- firewalls, servers, endpoints, applications -- into one central system
Encrypting logs before they are written to disk
Converting logs into a video format for review
questions.explain: Aggregation is simply centralizing logs from across the environment into one place.

questions.q: Why is normalization necessary before correlation can work effectively?
options: It isn't necessary -- correlation works equally well on raw, differently-formatted logs
Because every vendor formats logs differently, so events have to share a common schema before a correlation rule can reliably compare fields like source IP across them
Normalization is only needed for logs older than 90 days
Normalization replaces the need for aggregation entirely
questions.explain: A correlation rule looking for a field like 'source IP' needs that field to exist consistently across every log source, which is exactly what normalization provides.

questions.q: In the example from this lesson, what makes the failed-login-then-successful-login pattern worth investigating?
options: Failed logins are always malicious on their own
A failed login on one system followed shortly by a successful login on another system, from the same source IP, suggests credential testing or lateral movement
Successful logins are never logged by a SIEM
The two events happened on the same system, which is required for correlation
questions.explain: Neither event alone is unusual, but correlated together by shared source IP and close timing, they form a working incident theory.

questions.q: Which of these is a real example of a normalization schema mentioned in this lesson?
options: Common Event Format (CEF)
Structured Query Language (SQL)
Portable Network Graphics (PNG)
Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
questions.explain: Common Event Format (CEF) and the Elastic Common Schema (ECS) are real schemas used to give differently-formatted vendor logs a shared structure.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the three-step pipeline covered in this lesson?
options: Correlate, then aggregate, then normalize
Normalize, then correlate, then aggregate
Aggregate, then normalize, then correlate
The order doesn't matter as long as all three happen eventually
questions.explain: Logs must first be pulled into one place (aggregate), then mapped to a common schema (normalize), before they can be reliably compared across sources (correlate).
